# Wiring the Stack {#sec-wiring-stack}

A production LLM application in 2026 is assembled from parts that most teams
now recognize: clients and an agent runtime, a retrieval service, tools reached
through the Model Context Protocol, a sandbox for code the model writes, a model
gateway in front of hosted and self-hosted models, GPU compute, and
observability with evaluation. The earlier practical chapters treated these one
at a time: models (@sec-choosing-model), serving and compute
(@sec-serving-stack), training (@sec-training-practice), agents and sandboxes
(@sec-agents-practice), retrieval (@sec-retrieval-practice), and evaluation
(@sec-eval-practice). This chapter assembles them into one system in two halves.
The first half shows the assembled stack: a reference architecture with example
projects and products, the wire formats the components share, the model gateway
that most calls pass through, three archetype stacks, and the code at the seams.
The second half states the contracts that make the assembly releasable: a frozen
system identity, explicit compatibility, a state machine for each model
operation, bounded retries, separate credentials and effects, telemetry treated
as evidence, and a tested cutover.

The contract-first half comes from earlier systems work. Fielding described
networked systems in terms of constrained interfaces rather than particular
products [@fielding2000rest]. Sculley and colleagues later showed how glue code,
configuration, and undeclared consumers accumulate technical debt around
machine-learning systems [@sculley2015debt]. Breck and colleagues turned that
lesson into production-readiness tests [@breck2017mltest]. @sec-eval-practice
bound evaluation evidence to the exact system that was released. This chapter
makes the composition of the components testable, assembling in practice the
end-to-end stack that @sec-whole-stack traced.

## A reference architecture

@fig-reference-arch draws the stack by layer. Read from top to bottom, it is the
path of a request. A client calls the runtime; the runtime retrieves evidence,
calls tools through an MCP gateway, runs code in a sandbox, and calls models
through the model @gls-gateway, which forwards each call to a hosted API or to
self-hosted serving on the team's own GPUs. The observability and evaluation
layer at the bottom receives spans from every component and sends its own judge
calls back through the gateway. The color of each arrow is the credential that
the call carries.

```{figure}
//| figure: reference-stack
//| label: fig-reference-arch
//| fig-cap: "A reference stack for an LLM application, by layer, with example projects and products as of September 2026. Arrows are calls, and each arrow's color is the credential the call carries; the dashed bus carries OpenTelemetry GenAI spans, which grant no authority. Selecting a component shows what it does, example choices, and the contract in this chapter that governs it; with nothing selected, the readout groups the calls by credential. The named projects are examples, not recommendations."
```

Two gateways carry most of the traffic: the model gateway for model calls and
the MCP gateway for tool calls. The sandbox is the compute seam for code the
model writes, the counterpart of the model gateway's seam for model calls. Read
abstractly, every path in the figure has the same shape: a caller, an admission
decision, an adapter that turns the caller's contract into the provider's, and a
provider. Tool effects take a separately authorized path to an executor that
records each effect, retrieval returns identified evidence, and telemetry
observes every decision without granting any permission. The contracts in the
second half of the chapter are stated in these abstract terms, and selecting a
component in the figure names the contract that governs it.

No single product sits at the center of this architecture. The figure names
examples, and some products fill more than one box: agentgateway and Agent
Router each carry both model traffic and MCP traffic, and a hosted sandbox can
bundle its own egress control. Any box can be filled by a different product
that meets the same contract, so the durable part of the figure is the set of
boxes and the credentials on the arrows.

The credentials follow one rule: no application, agent, evaluation harness, or
sandbox holds a raw provider credential. Each holds a virtual key, a credential
that the gateway issues in place of the provider secret and scopes to a model
allowlist, a budget, and a rate limit. Rotating a provider secret or capping a
runaway agent then becomes a change at the gateway, with no client redeploy.
The same rule extends to the sandbox. Secrets stay outside it, and code inside
receives either a short-lived scoped token or a placeholder that the egress
proxy replaces with the real secret on the way to an allowlisted host
(@sec-security-authorization). In the figure, the provider-secret color appears
only on the gateway's calls to providers and on the egress proxy's calls out.

::: {.callout-note .dated}
## As of September 2026

E2B runs each sandbox in its own Firecracker microVM [@e2b2026runtime], as does
Vercel Sandbox [@vercel2026sandbox], while Modal virtualizes its compute jobs
with gVisor [@modal2026security]. The latest releases of the two open serving

[@vllm2026repo; @sglang2026serving44]. Two evaluation and observability tools

and Promptfoo announced that it is joining OpenAI through an acquisition
[@promptfoo2026openai].
:::

## The wire formats the components share

The components compose because they share a few wire formats, although their
features differ. Each format is a narrow interface that lets the
implementation behind it change without rewriting the callers in front of it.

Model calls travel in a small set of HTTP dialects. Three carry most traffic:
OpenAI Chat Completions (`/v1/chat/completions`), which open-weight servers such
as vLLM and SGLang expose; OpenAI Responses (`/v1/responses`); and Anthropic
Messages (`/v1/messages`). Coding harnesses are bound to a home dialect: Codex
speaks Responses and Claude Code speaks Messages. A gateway that accepts one
dialect and forwards another translates between them, and translation is where
meaning can be lost, in a tool-call convention, a thinking configuration, a
cache hint, or a field length. A gateway that reports what a translation dropped
lets the caller decide what to do; one that approximates silently changes the
system without leaving a record. The translating seam is also what lets a
self-hosted model and a hosted one sit behind a single model name.

Tool traffic converged further than model traffic did. The @gls-mcp lets one
tool server be reused by every agent host (@sec-agents-practice), and an MCP
gateway in front of the tool servers owns their credentials, the tool
allowlist, and the audit trail, as the model gateway does for model traffic.

Telemetry converged on the OpenTelemetry GenAI semantic conventions, a
vendor-neutral set of `gen_ai.*` span attributes for model calls, retrieval, and
agent steps (@sec-eval-practice). A component instrumented once can send the
same spans to Langfuse, Phoenix, or a general tracing backend without new
instrumentation.

::: {.callout-note .dated}
## As of September 2026

Codex accepts `responses` as the only wire protocol for a model provider
[@openai2026codexconfig]. Claude Code works through a gateway that exposes the
Anthropic Messages format, Bedrock InvokeModel, or Vertex rawPredict and
forwards the `anthropic-version` and `anthropic-beta` headers unchanged
[@anthropic2026gatewayprotocol], and Anthropic does not support routing Claude
Code to non-Claude models through a gateway [@anthropic2026claudecodegateway].
vLLM serves the Anthropic Messages API alongside its OpenAI-compatible API
[@vllm2026repo]. The current MCP revision, 2026-07-28, makes the protocol
stateless: it removes the initialization handshake and protocol-level sessions,
and every request carries its own protocol version and client capabilities
[@mcp2026release]. The GenAI conventions now live in their own repository and
are still marked as in development, with no tagged release, so an integration
pins the convention version it emits [@otel2026genaisemconv].
:::

## Three paths through the stack

The book built the stack along three paths, and the reference architecture is
where they meet. Walking each one through @fig-reference-arch shows how the
layers depend on one another.

### From chatbot to agent

A chatbot is one model call: a prompt in, a completion out. An agent wraps that
call in a loop. The model proposes a tool call, the runtime executes it and
returns the result, and the model chooses the next step, possibly for many
turns (@sec-agent-architectures, @sec-the-harness). Three additions turn the
first into the second, and each is a box in the figure.

- **Grounding through retrieval.** The agent retrieves current, private, or
  authoritative context instead of relying on what its weights hold
  (@sec-rag-retrieval, @sec-retrieval-practice). The common pipeline is
  @gls-hybrid-search: lexical BM25 scores and dense-vector similarity are
  merged by reciprocal rank fusion, which scores each document by adding
  $1/(k + \text{rank})$ over the ranked lists, with $k$ a small smoothing
  constant; a reranker, a model that rescores a short candidate list
  against the query, orders the result. The embedding model, which turns each
  text into a vector, and the rerank model are both called through the gateway,
  so they are keyed and budgeted like any other model call. Retrieval is usually cheaper and more faithful than filling a
  long context window, because every token of a long prompt is billed on every
  call (@sec-economics).
- **Actions through MCP and a sandbox.** Reading a result is the easy half.
  Once the agent runs code, calls an API, or writes a file, safety depends on
  the runtime more than on the model (@sec-agents-practice): a jailbreak filter
  at the gateway does nothing about a destructive shell command that the model
  was induced to emit. The @gls-sandbox bounds what such a command can reach,
  with default-deny egress, hard time limits, and human approval for
  irreversible actions (@sec-security-authorization).
- **Durable state through a checkpointer.** A long-running agent must survive a
  restart, so its state lives in a checkpointed store rather than in process
  memory (@sec-memory-systems). LangGraph saves graph state as checkpoints,
  with a Postgres implementation for production [@langgraph2026persistence],
  and Pydantic AI delegates durable execution to workflow engines such as
  Temporal, DBOS, Prefect, and Restate [@pydantic2026durable]. The checkpoint
  is what lets a person pause, inspect, and resume a task.

An agent cannot be more reliable than the gateway, serving, and sandbox layers
beneath it. Durable execution and checkpointing became standard framework
features for that reason: they are how a framework survives the failures of the
layers below it.

### From hosted models to owned ones

Most of a stack is inference: a fixed model served behind the gateway. The
gateway address that fronts a hosted model can also front a model the team
serves itself, and one it fine-tuned or post-trained (@sec-serving-stack,
@sec-training-practice). Moving along this path moves from renting capability
to owning it, and the gateway keeps the two interchangeable for every caller.

With a hosted API, the provider runs the inference server: batching, the
@gls-kv-cache, speculative decoding, and the accelerators
(@sec-serving-problem). The team sees them only as price terms, such as
cached-input pricing and priority tiers. When volume and control justify it,
the team serves open weights itself, commonly with vLLM, or with SGLang for
traffic that shares long prompt prefixes, and the per-token cost moves from an
invoice to a GPU bill that it schedules. Fine-tuning (@sec-sft-peft) adds a
training run on the compute layer, placed by a gang scheduler that starts all
of a job's workers together or none of them (@sec-orchestration-data-infra,
@sec-accelerators-networking). The variable that decides where a workload sits
is sustained utilization. Capacity paid by use costs nothing while idle, and
reserved capacity is cheaper only above a break-even share of the month, which
the accounting section below computes from two current quotes.

### From usage to evaluation

Every model and tool call the application makes is usage, and every unit of
usage can be observed and scored (@sec-eval-practice). A model that leads a
public leaderboard can still misbehave in a product, because the benchmark
measured a generic capability (@sec-benchmarks) while the product runs a
specific prompt over its own retrieval context inside an agent loop.

The loop has two halves that meet at the telemetry format. Observability
records the trace of a request: each model call, retrieval, and tool call, with
its inputs, outputs, timing, tokens, and cost. Evaluation scores those traces
with deterministic assertions, reference-based metrics, and a
@gls-llm-as-judge, a second model that grades the first against a calibrated
rubric (@sec-judging-holistic). A production trace that fails an online check
is promoted into the offline regression set, which gates the next release
(@sec-evaluating-agents). Because the application, the evaluation harness, and
the judge all call the gateway, an A/B comparison between two models is a
routing rule, and the judge runs on its own budget-capped key. The loop also
feeds the other two paths: evaluation data becomes training data, and failing
agent traces become the fixtures that harden the agent.

## The model gateway

A model gateway, also called an LLM gateway or AI gateway, is the control point
between application code and the model providers it calls. Its thinnest form is
a reverse proxy that accepts one API and forwards to many. Its job is to hold
five concerns in one place instead of scattering them through application code:
a unified API, custody of provider keys, cost tracking, routing and fallback,
and budgets and policy. Several gateways now also carry tool traffic over MCP
and agent-to-agent traffic over A2A, which makes them one policy point for most
of the stack's traffic.

| Name | What it is | Deployment and license | Fits |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **LiteLLM** | Python SDK and proxy that exposes more than 100 providers in the OpenAI format; virtual keys, budgets, spend tracking, load balancing, admin UI | Self-hosted; MIT outside an enterprise directory, plus a paid enterprise tier | The broadest provider coverage behind one self-hosted proxy |
| **OpenRouter** | Hosted aggregator: one endpoint, prepaid credits, bring-your-own-key | Managed service with a fee on credit purchases | Access to a large model catalog with nothing to operate |
| **Portkey** | Gateway with guardrails, retries and fallbacks, virtual keys, and caching | Open source (MIT), also offered as a hosted service | Guardrails and routing rules kept in the gateway |
| **agentgateway** | Rust proxy that acts as an LLM gateway, an MCP gateway, and an A2A gateway | Self-hosted; Apache 2.0; a Linux Foundation project | One policy point for model, tool, and agent-to-agent traffic |
| **Agent Router** (formerly Envoy AI Gateway) | Gateway on Envoy and Envoy Gateway: model routing, token-based rate limits and quotas, InferencePool support, MCP | Self-hosted on Kubernetes; Apache 2.0; an Agentic AI Foundation project | Platform teams that already run Envoy or the Kubernetes Gateway API |
| **Cloudflare AI Gateway** | Hosted gateway: analytics, logging, caching, rate limiting, retries and fallbacks, unified billing | Managed; core features free | Teams on Cloudflare that want no gateway to operate |
| **Bifrost** (Maxim AI) | Go gateway with one OpenAI-compatible API over more than 20 providers, fallbacks, load balancing, semantic caching | Self-hosted; Apache 2.0, with enterprise features | A self-hosted gateway built with low per-request overhead as a stated goal |
| **Lux** (latere.ai) | Go gateway: one address for the OpenAI, Anthropic, and Gemini dialects; sealed provider credentials; keys with model selectors, limits, and budgets; OIDC identity; an authorization webhook | Self-hosted; Apache 2.0; pre-release | The author's own gateway, listed with that disclosure and not as a neutral recommendation |

::: {.callout-note .dated}
## As of September 2026

LiteLLM's latest release is v1.102.1 [@litellm2026gateway]. OpenRouter charges
a 5.5 percent fee on credit purchases on its Standard plan and lists more than
500 models from more than 80 providers [@openrouter2026pricing]. Portkey's open
gateway is at v1.15.2 [@portkey2026gateway], and agentgateway at v1.5.0
[@agentgateway2026github44]. Envoy AI Gateway was renamed Agent Router in
September 2026, with the same code, maintainers, and license; its latest release
is v1.1.0 [@agentrouter2026]. Cloudflare's core AI Gateway features are free,
and Unified Billing adds a 5 percent fee on credits [@cloudflare2026aigatewaypricing].
Bifrost's README reports 11 µs of added overhead per request at 5,000 requests
per second, a measurement by its vendor [@bifrost2026maxim44]. Lux is
pre-release; v0.7.2 shipped on 24 September 2026 [@lux2026gateway44].
:::

Two distinctions matter more than feature lists: managed or self-hosted, and
model traffic only or model, tool, and agent traffic together.

- A **managed** gateway (OpenRouter, Cloudflare AI Gateway, Portkey's hosted
  service) needs no infrastructure and reaches a broad catalog quickly. It
  fits prototypes and small teams that accept provider keys and request
  metadata passing through a third party.
- A **self-hosted** gateway (LiteLLM, agentgateway, Agent Router, Bifrost)
  keeps provider secrets inside the team's environment and keeps request logs,
  data residency, and audit under the team's control. It fits regulated
  workloads and platform teams.
- A gateway that also carries **tool and agent traffic** (agentgateway, Agent
  Router) puts MCP calls and agent-to-agent calls under the same policy point
  as model calls, instead of adding tool governance to a model-only proxy
  later.

Gateway vendors publish latency and throughput figures measured under their own
conditions. For most workloads, provider and model latency exceed gateway
overhead by orders of magnitude, so per-request overhead rarely decides a
choice. What can decide it under agent load is the request rate at which the
gateway saturates, which depends on the implementation and on the work the
gateway does per request. A pass-through benchmark measures only the forwarding
path. A production gateway also authenticates, meters, applies policy, and
writes spend records, so the measurement that counts is the team's own
configuration at its own peak concurrency.

For a team that wants to hold its own keys and costs, the usual starting point
is a self-hosted gateway paired with an observability backend. Among
self-hosted gateways the distinctions above decide more than any benchmark:
LiteLLM for the widest provider coverage, agentgateway or Agent Router where
tool and agent traffic should pass the same policy point, and a managed gateway
where operating one is not worth the control. The contracts in the second half
of the chapter hold for whichever product fills the box. Lux appears in the
table because the author builds it.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Constraint arrow
The gateway is where a lower layer's economics reach the whole application.
Because every model call passes through one address, the per-token price of a
hosted frontier model (@sec-economics) and the per-token cost of self-hosted
serving (@sec-serving-problem) become routing rules instead of code changes.
Sending a hard step to an expensive model, or falling back to a cheaper one
under load, is decided once at the gateway, and every caller above it inherits
the decision.
:::

## Pick a reference stack

No single stack fits every team, but three archetypes cover most of them. The
rows are the layers of @fig-reference-arch; a team picks the column that
matches its constraints and reads down it. The entries are examples as of
September 2026 and starting points to adapt, not rankings.

| Layer | Lean, managed | Regulated, self-hosted | Cloud-native Kubernetes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Model** | Hosted frontier APIs (Anthropic, OpenAI, Google) with pinned model IDs | Hosted models for hard steps, self-hosted open weights for bulk traffic | The same, with open-weight models served in the cluster |
| **Gateway** | OpenRouter or Cloudflare AI Gateway | LiteLLM, agentgateway, or Bifrost, self-hosted, with virtual keys and budgets | Agent Router or agentgateway in the cluster |
| **Serving** | None operated; the API is the server | vLLM behind an OpenAI-compatible endpoint, with FP8 weights and prefix caching | vLLM or SGLang, with llm-d or NVIDIA Dynamo for cache-aware routing at scale |
| **Agent runtime** | OpenAI Agents SDK or Claude Agent SDK | LangGraph with a checkpointer, or Pydantic AI with durable execution | LangGraph with a Postgres checkpointer |
| **Sandbox** | E2B or Vercel Sandbox, hosted microVMs | Self-hosted Firecracker or gVisor with default-deny egress | Sandboxes in the same cluster under gVisor, with scoped tokens |
| **Retrieval** | A managed search service (turbopuffer, Pinecone) with Cohere Embed and Rerank | Postgres with pgvector and pgvectorscale, open embeddings such as BGE-M3 | Qdrant with hybrid queries and an open reranker |
| **Evaluation and observability** | LangSmith or Braintrust, hosted | Self-hosted Langfuse, with Promptfoo or DeepEval in CI | Phoenix or another OpenTelemetry backend, with DeepEval in CI |
| **Compute** | GPUs billed by use (Modal, Baseten, Fireworks, Together) | Committed capacity from a neocloud (CoreWeave, Lambda), with Slurm and Kubernetes | Kubernetes with Kueue quotas and Volcano or KAI Scheduler gang scheduling |

::: {.callout-note .dated}
## As of September 2026

Cohere's current retrieval models are `embed-v4.0` and the `rerank-v4.0-pro`
and `rerank-v4.0-fast` rerankers [@cohere2026models]. Qdrant fuses dense and
sparse results in a single hybrid query and describes reciprocal rank fusion as
the safe default [@qdrant2026hybrid]. Modal bills GPUs per second of use,
listing an NVIDIA H100 at 0.001097 dollars per second [@modal2026pricing44].
:::

The advice under the table outlasts its entries. Keep the number of new moving
parts small. Spend the quality budget where it pays: retrieval and reranking
before a more elaborate vector database, calibrated judges before more
benchmarks. Keep every layer reachable through the shared wire formats so that
each one can be swapped, and hard-code no single vendor. The archetype a team
starts in is rarely the one it ends in, and the wire formats and contracts are
what keep the migration cheap.

## Wiring the seams in code

The glue that matters is the code at the seams, the few lines that make the
layers interchangeable. Two snippets show the pattern: a gateway configuration
that puts a hosted and a self-hosted model behind one name with a fallback, and
an agent that reaches that name with a virtual key.

The gateway configuration exposes one alias, `smart`, that fails over from
hosted models to a self-hosted one, so the application never learns which
model served a request. The shape is illustrative rather than any one product's
schema: LiteLLM writes it as a YAML model list, while other gateways bind the
routing strategy to a virtual key through an admin API or a dashboard. The
seam the application sees is the same either way.

```yaml
# Illustrative gateway configuration: one alias, two hosted targets, and a
# self-hosted fallback. Each gateway has its own schema; this is the shape.
models:
  - alias: smart                     # the name the application requests
    target: anthropic/claude-opus-5-5
    api_key: ${ANTHROPIC_API_KEY}    # the provider secret stays in the gateway
  - alias: smart                     # same alias, second provider
    target: openai/gpt-6-sol
    api_key: ${OPENAI_API_KEY}
    upstream_api: responses          # tool calls with reasoning need Responses
  - alias: local                     # self-hosted, behind the same address
    target: vllm/open-weight-model
    base_url: http://vllm.inference.svc:8000/v1

routing:
  smart:
    strategy: fallback               # targets prequalified for one capability profile
    fallback: [local]
    retries: 2                       # the gateway is the single retry owner
# Virtual keys, budgets, and spend caps are issued through the admin API,
# not in this file.
```

The agent holds a gateway virtual key, not a provider secret. It retrieves
context through a tool and never learns which model answered. The tool here is
an in-process MCP server for brevity; in production it sits behind the MCP
gateway over HTTP and the agent code barely changes, because MCP is a wire
protocol rather than a library interface. The sketch uses the Claude Agent SDK
[@anthropic2026claudeagentsdk44], whose custom tools are named
`mcp__<server>__<tool>` and run without a permission prompt when listed in
`allowed_tools` [@anthropic2026agentsdktools].

```python
from claude_agent_sdk import ClaudeAgentOptions, create_sdk_mcp_server, query, tool

@tool("search_docs", "Retrieve grounding context for a query", {"q": str})
async def search_docs(args):
    # hybrid retrieval and rerank; the embedding and rerank calls use the gateway too
    hits = await retriever.hybrid_search(args["q"], top_k=8)
    return {"content": [{"type": "text", "text": "\n\n".join(h.text for h in hits)}]}

rag = create_sdk_mcp_server(name="rag", version="1.0.0", tools=[search_docs])

options = ClaudeAgentOptions(
    mcp_servers={"rag": rag},
    allowed_tools=["mcp__rag__search_docs"],  # pre-approved; other tools still ask
    env={
        "ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL": "https://llm-gateway.internal",  # the one model address
        "ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN": virtual_key,  # scoped gateway key, not a provider secret
        "CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_RETRIES": "0",       # retries belong to the gateway
    },
)

async for message in query(prompt="Summarize our refund policy and cite the source.",
                           options=options):
    print(message)
```

The evaluation harness follows the same discipline. A Promptfoo configuration
points its provider's `apiBaseUrl` at the gateway and names the harness's own
key with `apiKeyEnvar` [@promptfoo2026openaiprovider], and the judge is a model
from a different family on a separately budgeted key (@sec-eval-practice).
Model calls, tool calls, retrieval, and judging all meet at two addresses, the
model gateway and the MCP gateway, and all emit the same span format. That is
what makes the assembly one system rather than several tools placed side by
side.

Integrations tend to break at the translation in a seam, and on small
wire-level constraints rather than on large incompatibilities: a field-length
limit, a request shape one model generation accepts and the next rejects, or a
parameter whose meaning changed. The check that catches these is cheap. Each new
pairing of model and harness is smoke-tested with one tool-bearing request
before anything relies on it, which is the smallest form of the conformance
fixtures described later in this chapter.

::: {.callout-note .dated}
## As of September 2026

OpenAI's Responses API limits `safety_identifier`, which replaces the
deprecated `user` field, to 64 characters, so a gateway that receives longer
session identifiers from a harness has to hash or shorten them
[@openai2026responsescreate]. Starting with GPT-5.4, Chat Completions does not
support tool calls combined with a reasoning effort other than `none`, so a
gateway that forwards an agent's tool-bearing Chat Completions traffic to a
current reasoning model has to switch it to Responses
[@openai2026migrateresponses]. Anthropic replaced the fixed thinking budget
with adaptive thinking steered by an effort level: Claude 4.7 and later models
reject the budget form with a 400 error, while Claude 4.5 models, including
Haiku 4.5, accept only the budget form [@anthropic2026thinkingtroubleshooting].
A gateway serving both generations therefore needs a capability profile per
model rather than one translation rule. The effort level is guidance, not a
quota: at every level the model decides per request whether to think, and a
request that only processes tool results can skip thinking even at the highest
levels [@anthropic2026steeringthinking].
:::

The architecture so far says what connects to what. Connected products become
one releasable system when every boundary has a contract, every component that
affects behavior has an identity, and a failed release has a tested way back.
The rest of the chapter states those contracts, and each box in
@fig-reference-arch names the one that governs it.

## Freeze the integration release

The deliverable of the second half is an **integration release**: a versioned
statement of what is connected, what each connection means, who owns it, and
what evidence makes the assembled behavior safe to release. It starts from the
release decision rather than from a product inventory. The decision names the
capability being released, its users and tenants, its permitted data classes
and effects, its quality and operational thresholds, and its rollback trigger.
The release then freezes a **system fingerprint** containing the model
revision, prompt revision, retrieval snapshot, tool schema, policy revision,
router configuration, telemetry schema, and executable artifact digests. A
model name alone cannot identify the system that produced an answer.

An integration release owns two records. The **system manifest** identifies the
assembled system. The **boundary contract** defines each edge between a producer
and a consumer. Neither record may contain mutable aliases such as `latest`.

| Record | Required fields | Release question |
| --- | --- | --- |
| System manifest | application, model, prompt, retrieval, tool, policy, router, telemetry, and artifact revisions | Can this exact behavior be identified again? |
| Topology | every producer, consumer, protocol version, transport, and owner | Does every live edge have an accountable owner? |
| Capability profile | native, adapter-emulated, lossy, or unsupported behavior | What meaning changes at an adapter? |
| Trust contract | principal, workload, tenant, authority, audience, scope, and data class | May this caller send this data or cause this effect? |
| Failure contract | deadline, cancellation, retry owner, idempotency scope, error mapping, and backpressure | Where does failure stop, and who may retry? |
| Evidence contract | telemetry, conformance result, migration state, acceptance evidence, and rollback revision | What proves the release and restores the last good one? |

The manifest itself should be signed or otherwise integrity-protected. It
records a software bill of materials, build provenance, container and binary
digest values, schema revisions, policy bundles, and the exact route table.
in-toto supplies a model for verifiable supply-chain steps
[@torresarias2019intoto], while SLSA defines progressively stronger provenance
requirements [@slsa2026spec]. These controls make the artifact that was tested
distinguishable from a later substitution. Whether that artifact behaves
correctly is still established by the tests.

## Separate the planes

The stack has three planes with different permissions and failure modes.

- The **data plane** carries model requests, typed stream events, retrieval
  evidence, tool proposals, and tool results.
- The **control plane** admits requests and applies routing, budgets, capability
  constraints, authorization policy, and overload rules.
- The **management plane** changes route tables, credentials, policy bundles,
  schemas, and integration releases.

A model @gls-gateway can enforce data- and control-plane policy for model
traffic, and every other boundary enforces its own. Retrieval authorization
belongs at the retrieval service. A tool executor must authorize its own
resources. Management-plane changes require a narrower administrative path than
ordinary inference. A single proxy process may implement several roles, but the
contracts and privileges must remain separate.

## Make compatibility explicit

Two APIs with similar JSON shapes can carry different semantics. HTTP defines
transport semantics [@rfc9110http]; server-sent events define stream framing
[@whatwg2026sse]. Neither defines a provider's tool-call lifecycle, refusal
state, structured-output subset, usage counters, retention behavior, or safety
policy. An adapter must therefore publish a versioned **capability profile**.

Each requested capability is recorded in one of four states:

- **native**: the provider implements the declared meaning;
- **adapter-emulated**: the adapter preserves the declared postcondition;
- **lossy**: the adapter changes meaning, and the caller has explicitly accepted
  that downgrade;
- **unsupported**: admission rejects the request before upstream work begins.

The profile should declare modalities, endpoint and state model, tool and
parallel-call semantics, the supported JSON Schema dialect and subset, typed
stream events, context and output limits, usage fields, region, retention, and
policy restrictions. JSON Schema is a language family with identifiable
dialects, and a provider may implement only a subset of its keywords
[@jsonschema2020core]. Translation has only three defensible outcomes: preserve,
perform an explicitly accepted downgrade, or reject. Silently dropping a tool,
truncating an identifier, or coercing an unknown field is an undeclared change
of meaning.

Routing follows the same discipline. The router first filters by hard
constraint: capability, tenant policy, data residency, retention, region, and
authority. It then ranks the eligible candidates by measured quality, latency,
availability, or cost. Every accepted operation resolves to an immutable
provider, model revision, adapter revision, capability-profile revision, and
route-policy revision. Experiments and canaries use sticky assignment, so
repeated work stays on one system.

## Define the model-operation state machine

The runtime treats a request as a **logical operation** containing a verified
tenant, `operation_id`, payload digest, remaining deadline, requirements, and
policy revision. Admission either rejects it or records the immutable route
decision. Each upstream call is a **physical attempt** beneath that logical
operation.

The operation passes through these steps:

1. Receive and authenticate the operation.
2. Validate its schema and capability requirements.
3. Admit it under tenant, budget, region, and policy constraints.
4. Resolve and record an immutable route.
5. Open an upstream attempt and normalize its frames into a versioned
   **typed event stream** with operation, attempt, and sequence identifiers.
6. Accumulate streamed tool fragments without executing them.
7. On a terminal tool block, parse the complete arguments, validate them against
   the pinned schema, authorize the exact effect, and execute once.
8. Preserve refusal, incomplete output, cancellation, partial output, error, and
   normal completion as distinct terminal outcomes.

Stream chunks are fragments of a response, and an unknown event type among them
is retained or surfaced for forward compatibility instead of being reinterpreted
as text. Partial tool arguments must never execute. A structured result
receives final validation against the declared JSON Schema profile only after
assembly. Refusal, truncation, transport failure, and schema violation each
produce a separate invalid outcome rather than a plausible-looking object.

After caller-visible output, an automatic retry can duplicate or contradict the
stream, so the runtime does not replay transparently once output is visible. It
propagates cancellation and the remaining deadline downstream, and when a caller
disconnects it stops reading and cancels the upstream attempt. Every admitted
operation must reach a terminal state through finite attempts, a finite
deadline, and bounded resources.

## Normalize errors without hiding causes

Errors travel in a stable machine-readable envelope based on RFC 9457
[@rfc9457problem], with media type `application/problem+json`. The envelope
carries a stable problem type, the upstream error category in a form safe to
expose, HTTP status, provider code, upstream request ID, operation ID, attempt
number, whether output was partial, whether the operation is retryable, and any
`Retry-After` value. The original cause is preserved in protected diagnostics.

The human-readable detail field is for people, and no retry decision parses it.
Authentication, authorization, invalid input, unsupported capability, policy
refusal, and exhausted quota are normally not retryable. Overload and transient
transport failures may be retryable only under the operation's budget and
deadline.

## Bound retries and overload

Nested client, gateway, adapter, and provider retries create **retry
amplification**. Here $\ell$ denotes a retrying layer and $r_\ell$ its maximum
retry count. The maximum number of physical attempts generated by one logical
operation is

$$
A_{\max}=\prod_{\ell=1}^{L}(1+r_\ell),
$$

where $L$ is the number of independently retrying layers. Two retries at each of
three layers can create $3^3=27$ attempts. The design therefore assigns a single
**retry owner**, the one layer permitted to retry. It obeys a total attempt
limit and remaining deadline, honors `Retry-After`, and uses bounded exponential
backoff with jitter. Every physical attempt is recorded, even when the logical
operation succeeds. Latency tails in large fan-out systems are a further reason
for these controls [@dean2013tail]. @fig-wiring-retry-amplification shows how
much of that bound a failing provider receives.

```{figure}
//| figure: retry-amplification
//| label: fig-wiring-retry-amplification
//| fig-cap: "Physical attempts generated by one logical operation when $L$ layers each retry up to $r$ times, against a single retry owner. The tree outlines every call each layer can issue, with $A_{\max}$ physical attempts in the bottom row ($\prod_\ell (1 + r_\ell)$ when every layer retries, $1 + r$ with one owner), and fills the calls made in one seeded run at the chosen failure probability $p$. The chart gives the expected physical attempts per logical operation, $(1 - p^{A_{\max}})/(1 - p)$, with attempts failing independently: as $p$ approaches 1, when the provider is already failing, nested retries send up to $A_{\max}$ times the offered load. Under real overload the failure rate rises with that load, which is how a retry storm forms; backoff, deadlines, and `Retry-After` are not modeled."
```

An idempotency key is an application-level contract; HTTP by itself does not
deliver a request exactly once. The key is bound to tenant, route class,
operation key, canonical payload digest, and time to live. Reusing a key with a
different payload is an error. Where the provider or target cannot deduplicate,
the contract states that exactly-once is not guaranteed. A side-effecting tool
needs its own effect-level key and receipt; a model-request key cannot make the
tool idempotent.

Overload controls must also be bounded: per-tenant concurrency, queue length,
stream buffer, input and output tokens, and tool fan-out. A bounded queue exposes
backpressure instead of turning latency into hidden memory growth. Excess work
is shed with the appropriate `429` or `503` and a `Retry-After` value, and
circuit breakers and retry budgets keep recovery traffic from becoming a retry
storm.

Fallback changes the system identity. A fallback candidate must be prequalified
inside a declared compatibility class, the set of candidates whose capability
profiles meet the operation's requirements, and must satisfy the same hard
policy and data constraints. The new route decision is recorded. After visible
output, or after a side effect whose result is ambiguous, the runtime must not
switch systems silently.

## Keep identity, credentials, and effects separate

A gateway credential, a workload identity, a delegated user token, and a
downstream provider secret answer different questions. Short-lived workload
identity and OAuth token exchange [@rfc8693tokenexchange] are the preferred
mechanisms. Each token is bound to an audience, scope, verified tenant, subject
or actor, and time to live. Every resource server validates its own audience,
and a token issued for one resource is never passed through to another.

The **virtual key** introduced with the reference architecture implements
model-budget and routing policy; tool calls are authorized separately, at the
tool boundary. Where a provider supports only a static
secret, a broker holds that secret and substitutes it only at an allowed egress
boundary. The application and sandbox should not receive the raw provider
secret. Zero-trust guidance similarly treats network location as insufficient
authority [@nist2020zerotrust].

### Tools and MCP

The @gls-mcp standardizes host, client, and server messages over JSON-RPC and
supports capability negotiation, discovery, and tool schemas [@mcp2026spec44].
Discovering a tool grants no authority to call it, and a tool annotation is
untrusted metadata that cannot establish that a call is safe. The integration
pins the MCP protocol revision, transport, and negotiated capabilities, and it
authorizes each invocation under the controls in @sec-security-authorization.

The trusted runtime should perform this sequence:

1. Authenticate user and workload; derive the tenant from verified identity.
2. Validate the selected tool name against an allowlist and canonicalize the
   complete arguments against pinned input and output schemas.
3. Classify the effect as read, reversible write, or irreversible/external.
4. Authorize the principal, workload, tenant, tool revision, resource, audience,
   canonical arguments, effect class, and policy revision; bind expiring consent
   or approval where required.
5. Append an intent record, broker a least-privilege credential, and execute with
   an effect-level idempotency key.
6. Persist an effect receipt before advancing the workflow checkpoint; validate
   and redact the result before returning it.

After an ambiguous timeout, the runtime queries the receipt or the target state
instead of retrying a non-idempotent effect. Canceling a call leaves any effect
that has already happened in place. Parallel calls require independent call IDs
and receipts. A tool result must retain its originating call ID so the runtime
cannot attach it to the wrong proposal.

A @gls-sandbox reduces blast radius, the damage an inappropriate action can
do; deciding whether an action is appropriate remains the job of authorization.
Its threat model should bound filesystem access, syscalls, processes, CPU,
memory, disk, wall-clock time, workspace lifetime, and network access. The
sandbox enforces both an egress allowlist and a resource allowlist, and it
resolves and validates DNS and every redirect hop, blocking private, link-local,
and metadata endpoints.

### Retrieval and evidence

Retrieval is authorized before candidate documents cross the retrieval service's
boundary. Every result should carry an evidence ID, source and corpus revision,
index revision, authorization decision, and tenant boundary. Cache, checkpoint,
session, task, and deduplication keys must include tenant and system-policy
identity. @sec-retrieval-practice develops the underlying evidence contract.

## Treat telemetry as evidence

W3C Trace Context supplies correlation identifiers across services
[@w3c2021tracecontext]. Those identifiers carry no authority, so principal,
tenant, and permission are never inferred from `traceparent` or from baggage,
the key-value context that travels with a trace. Baggage has no built-in
integrity and must contain no secret, personal data, or authorization decision;
each trust boundary allowlists and strips it.

The trace records the operation ID, physical attempt ID, route and adapter
revisions, capability decision, error category, tool intent and receipt,
evidence IDs, and terminal outcome. Missing telemetry, exporter loss, sampling,
and redaction failure are reported as well. A trace is partial evidence and
cannot by itself show whether an effect occurred (@sec-eval-practice).

## Account for the accepted task

The unit of accounting is the whole accepted task, a task whose result passed
acceptance, rather than a model-call subtotal. Cost includes every physical
attempt, model usage, retrieval, tool execution, any judge model that grades the
result, infrastructure, and human review. Latency is the elapsed time of the
root operation; parallel child durations are not summed. Prices use the exact
response model, region, billing time, currency, and price-catalog revision
rather than a mutable alias
(@sec-economics, @sec-serving-problem).

For task $q$, a useful accounting identity is

$$
C_q=\sum_{a\in\mathcal{A}_q}\sum_{m\in\mathcal{M}_a}u_{a,m}p_m(v_a,\rho_a,t_a,k_a)
    +C_{\mathrm{infra}}+C_{\mathrm{human}},
$$

where $\mathcal{A}_q$ is the set of physical attempts, $\mathcal{M}_a$ contains
disjoint billing meters for attempt $a$, $u_{a,m}$ is usage on meter $m$, and
$p_m$ is its price for response-model revision $v_a$, region $\rho_a$, billing
time $t_a$, and price-catalog revision $k_a$. The remaining terms cover shared
infrastructure and human review. Disjoint meters prevent cached or reasoning
subtotals from being counted twice.

Build-versus-rent is likewise settled by a measured crossover point, which
differs from one contract to the next. The two prices in the chart below are
editable placeholders; a real comparison replaces them with current,
contract-specific values, and the defaults carry no recommendation.

```{figure}
//| figure: reserved-breakeven
//| label: fig-wiring-a-2026-stack-cost-crossover
//| fig-cap: "Monthly cost against GPU-hours used in a 720-hour month, with the chapter's placeholder prices, which the controls edit. Serverless billing rises with each used hour, $r \cdot h$; the reserved bill $F$ is flat, so the two break even at $h^* = F/r$, which the top axis reads as a share of the month, the fraction the runnable below computes. The bars split the reserved bill between the hours used and the hours left idle at the chosen use. When $F/r$ exceeds 720 hours, the reserved bill costs more at any use within the month. A decision replaces both prices with current quotes and also counts operations and reliability costs, which the figure leaves out."
```

:::: {.runnable}
```python
def crossover_utilization(serverless_rate, reserved_monthly, hours=720):
    """Return the utilization fraction where pay-per-use equals the flat bill."""
    if serverless_rate <= 0 or reserved_monthly < 0 or hours <= 0:
        raise ValueError("rates and hours must define a non-negative comparison")
    return reserved_monthly / (serverless_rate * hours)

example = crossover_utilization(4.0, 1440.0)
assert abs(example - 0.5) < 1e-12
print(f"illustrative crossover = {example:.0%}")
```
::::

@sec-scaling-laws and @sec-accelerators-networking explain why workload shape,
memory, batching, and hardware efficiency matter beyond the simple curve.

## Test every boundary, including its failure paths

Every adapter and boundary should pass the same conformance fixtures before it
joins a release.

| Fixture | Required assertion |
| --- | --- |
| Unary request | exact request identity, terminal status, usage, and error mapping |
| Stream interruption | ordered typed events, partial status, no replay after visible output |
| Tool arguments | no execution before complete parse, schema validation, authorization, and call-ID binding |
| Structured output | final local validation; refusal, incomplete, and schema error remain distinct |
| Rate limit and overload | `Retry-After`, bounded queue behavior, cancellation, and correct `429` or `503` |
| Retry and fallback | one retry owner, finite attempts, compatible fallback, and changed system identity |
| Tenant isolation | wrong-audience token, cross-tenant cache or handle, stale approval, and secret leakage all fail closed |
| Telemetry | operation/attempt correlation, route decision, missing telemetry, and redaction are visible |

Negative fixtures cover unknown stream events, duplicate delivery, a worker
crash after commit but before receipt, malicious tool output, schema drift, DNS
rebinding, redirect to a metadata endpoint, filesystem escape, and runaway
process creation. A successful demo exercises none of these paths.

## Cut over as a protocol

Migration is itself an integration, and the cutover runs in a fixed order.
Adapter contract tests come first. New read-only behavior then runs in shadow
mode, with no side effects. A sticky canary follows and keeps each task or
tenant on one fingerprint, and traffic ramps only while quality, security,
latency, error, and cost gates hold. Route and policy changes are published
atomically. The last-known-good manifest stays deployable, and rollback is
tested before the first canary receives traffic.

```{dot}
//| label: fig-cutover-path
//| fig-cap: "A reversible integration cutover. Contract tests precede a side-effect-free shadow, sticky canary, staged ramp, and release. Any failed gate restores the last-known-good manifest."
digraph {
  bgcolor="transparent"; rankdir=TB; nodesep=0.16; ranksep=0.24;
  node [shape=box, style="rounded,filled", fontname="Helvetica", fontsize=9,
        color="#6b7280", fontcolor="#6b7280", fillcolor="#f1ece1"];
  edge [fontname="Helvetica", fontsize=9, color="#6b7280", arrowsize=0.65];
  tests [label="Contract tests"];
  shadow [label="Shadow"];
  canary [label="Sticky canary"];
  ramp [label="Staged ramp"];
  release [label="Release"];
  lkg [label="Last-known-good"];
  tests -> shadow -> canary -> ramp -> release;
  shadow -> lkg [label="fail"];
  canary -> lkg [label="fail"];
  ramp -> lkg [label="fail"];
}
```

The failure matrix gives each failure a detection signal and an owned
containment and recovery action.

| Failure | Detection | Containment and recovery |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Silent capability loss | capability and conformance mismatch | reject admission; restore prior adapter |
| Retry storm | attempt amplification and queue alarms | disable nested retries; shed load |
| Credential leak | secret canary or audience violation | revoke, rotate, and quarantine evidence |
| Cross-tenant access | authorization and isolation fixture | fail closed; invalidate affected caches and handles |
| Partial tool execution | intent without a matching effect receipt | query target state; reconcile rather than replay |
| Configuration drift | signed-manifest or digest mismatch | stop rollout; restore atomic last-known-good state |
| Missing telemetry | export and coverage SLO breach | halt evidence-dependent release decisions |

## The release lifecycle

The complete workflow is short enough to rehearse:

1. State the capability, population, constraints, and rollback trigger.
2. Inventory producers, consumers, owners, trust boundaries, and data classes.
3. Freeze the system fingerprint and signed manifest.
4. Publish capability, identity, failure, effect, and evidence contracts.
5. Implement adapters that preserve, explicitly downgrade, or reject.
6. Assign one retry owner and bound deadlines, queues, and concurrency.
7. Bind credentials and tool effects to verified identity and tenant policy.
8. Run protocol, policy, isolation, failure, and supply-chain conformance tests.
9. Measure accepted-task quality, latency, cost, and missing evidence.
10. Shadow without side effects, then run a sticky canary and staged ramp.
11. Publish the atomic manifest and retain the tested rollback revision.
12. Record owners, known gaps, expiry, and requalification triggers.

The output is an integration release record: the exact manifest, boundary
contracts, test evidence, accepted degradations, rollout state, known gaps,
owners, expiry, and rollback procedure.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Constraint arrow
An upper layer cannot recover semantics that a lower boundary silently removed.
Provider limits constrain adapters; adapters constrain routing; routing and
authorization constrain the application; the assembled fingerprint constrains
what an evaluation result can claim. The lowest boundary that knows about a loss
is the one that has to make it visible.
:::

::: {.callout-important}
## What's contested
Some teams expose one provider-shaped API everywhere; others keep provider-native
clients behind a narrower domain interface. Some centralize admission in one
gateway that also carries tool and agent-to-agent traffic; others keep model,
tool, and agent traffic on separate proxies, so that a fault or a compromise in
one does not reach the others. Either can work, and each topology has to meet
the same requirements: explicit semantic loss, least authority, bounded
failure, immutable identity, end-to-end evidence, and tested rollback. The
reference stack in this chapter is a snapshot of named products; the contracts
are the part expected to outlast it.
:::
